about: Criteria you can add to your Scorecard. 'calc' criteria are scored by the Scorecard from inputs; 'judgment' criteria you score 1-5 against anchors you can rewrite. Anchor 1 = the worst you'd still accept (anything worse belongs in a gate), 5 = the best you could realistically find, 3 = solidly OK. 'starter: true' marks the ten-criterion starter set.

criteria.name: Revenue predictability
criteria.hint: How steady the revenue stream is, not whether each customer returns. A steady flow of one-off buyers counts.

anchors.1: Lumpy: a few big-ticket, discretionary sales or projects make or break the month.
anchors.2: A meaningful share of revenue comes from big-ticket items or projects.
anchors.3: A steady flow of everyday, low-ticket, high-volume purchases.
anchors.4: A strong base of repeat customers, plus some contracts or memberships.
anchors.5: Mostly contracts, memberships, subscriptions or a documented base of regulars.

criteria.brokerQ: What share of revenue is recurring (contracts, memberships, regulars)? Can I see monthly revenue for the last 24 months?
criteria.clues: "recurring", "membership", "contracts", "repeat customers", average ticket size, transaction counts

criteria.name: Tourism & seasonality
criteria.hint: Would a bad tourist season or a slow quarter hurt? Think about your region's own seasons and weather.

anchors.1: Mostly visitor-driven, or about 40%+ of revenue lands in one season.
anchors.2: Mostly local, but a big seasonal swing (one season ~30-40% of revenue) or ~30-40% visitors.
anchors.3: Mostly local with a noticeable seasonal swing, or roughly 20-30% visitors.
anchors.4: Local, with a mild seasonal bump (e.g. holidays) and few visitors.
anchors.5: Local, needs-based customers. Flat all year.

criteria.brokerQ: Monthly revenue for the last 2-3 years? Roughly what share of customers are visitors rather than locals?

criteria.name: Track record
criteria.hint: Calculated from years open and the revenue trend. Declining revenue is handled by a gate, not here.

anchors.1: Young (under the first year band), revenue flat.
anchors.3: Middle of the year bands, revenue flat.
anchors.5: Long history (top year band), steady or growing.

criteria.brokerQ: What year was the business founded? Revenue and SDE for each of the last 3 years?

criteria.name: Team in place
criteria.hint: Who does the work when you're not there?

anchors.1: Owner plus about one part-timer. The owner is the labor.
anchors.2: A few staff, but the owner works most shifts and runs everything.
anchors.3: Staff do most of the work; the owner is the glue. No formal manager.
anchors.4: A lead or assistant manager handles daily operations; the owner fills gaps and does admin.
anchors.5: A manager runs day-to-day with trained staff. The owner only oversees.

criteria.brokerQ: Who runs day-to-day? Staff count, roles and tenure. Is there a manager?

criteria.name: Owner dependence
criteria.hint: Would the regulars miss the old owner more than the business? (If the owner IS the product, that's a gate.)

anchors.1: Many customers come for the owner, who holds most key customer and supplier relationships.
anchors.2: Several key customers or suppliers deal only with the owner.
anchors.3: The owner is a face of the business, but key relationships are shared.
anchors.4: The owner is known, but staff handle most relationships; few customers would follow the owner out.
anchors.5: Customers buy the brand. Staff hold the relationships.

criteria.brokerQ: Which customer and supplier relationships are personal to the owner? How many hours does the owner work, doing what?

criteria.name: Transition support
criteria.hint: Often a tiebreaker. A low weight means tiebreaker, not irrelevant.

anchors.1: Seller gone at close, nothing documented.
anchors.2: A week or so of handover, little written down, staff new or few.
anchors.3: 2-4 weeks of training, plus some documentation or long-tenured staff.
anchors.4: Seller offers 1-6 months of help, and key processes are written down.
anchors.5: Seller stays 6-12 months to train or consult, and processes are written down.

criteria.brokerQ: Will the seller stay on to train or consult, and for how long? What's documented?

criteria.name: Deal math
criteria.hint: Calculated: the lower of your take-home band and your loan-coverage (DSCR) band at the asking price.

anchors.1: Pays you your minimum salary or less; loan payments barely fit, or don't.
anchors.3: Comfortable take-home and a reasonable safety margin on the loan.
anchors.5: Pays well above what you need, with loan payments that fit with room to spare.

criteria.brokerQ: SDE (or EBITDA plus total owner pay) for the last 3 years, with add-backs itemized?

criteria.name: Operator upside
criteria.hint: Usually '?' from a listing. Count only gaps you can see evidence of; broker-promised 'growth potential' earns nothing.

anchors.1: Already well run and modern. Little for you to add (not bad if you want passive income).
anchors.2: Mostly well run; a gap or two to tidy up, but no real lever.
anchors.3: Room to modernize some things; decently run.
anchors.4: Clear gaps in one or two areas you know well (e.g. no online sales, manual scheduling).
anchors.5: Specific, visible gaps right in your wheelhouse that plausibly raise earnings when fixed.

criteria.brokerQ: What would the owner change with more time or money? What systems run the business today (POS, booking, books)?

criteria.name: Commute burden
criteria.hint: Calculated from one-way drive time and how often you'd need to be there.

anchors.1: At the edge of your limit for how often you'd need to be there.
anchors.3: Partway between close to home and your limit.
anchors.5: Close to home, or rarely needed on site.

criteria.brokerQ: Where exactly is the business located? How often does the owner actually need to be on site?

criteria.name: Premises
criteria.hint: Calculated: lease security x how much the business depends on its location.

anchors.1: A storefront that depends on its spot, with under 5 years left and no right to renew.
anchors.3: A location-dependent business with 5-10 years left including options.
anchors.5: Owned, a long lease with options, or a business that could easily move.

criteria.brokerQ: Lease term remaining, renewal options, current rent, and will the landlord assign it or sign a new lease?

criteria.name: Customer concentration
criteria.hint: Rarely visible in a listing; expect '?' until you see documents. Consider leaving it for the documents stage.

anchors.1: One customer is about a third of revenue, or the top three are more than half.
anchors.3: The largest customer is 10-15% of revenue; the rest are spread out.
anchors.5: No customer is more than a few percent of revenue.

criteria.brokerQ: What share of revenue comes from the top 1, 3 and 10 customers? Any of them under contract?

criteria.name: License & permit transfer
criteria.hint: Who holds the licenses, permits or qualifier the business runs on, and do they transfer?

anchors.1: The business runs on a license only the seller holds, with no clear path to transfer or replace it.
anchors.3: Licenses can be re-issued to a new owner or held by an employee, with some paperwork and lead time.
anchors.5: No special licensing, or licenses that transfer with the business as a matter of course.

criteria.brokerQ: Which licenses, permits or qualifiers does the business operate under, who holds each, and do they transfer?

criteria.name: Reputation & online presence
criteria.hint: Five minutes on review sites and the business's own website.

anchors.1: Poor or thin reviews, no usable website or listings.
anchors.3: Decent reviews and a basic web presence.
anchors.5: Strong, recent reviews; a brand people search for by name.

criteria.brokerQ: Does the business own its domain, social accounts and review profiles, and do they transfer with the sale?

criteria.name: Capital needs
criteria.hint: How much money the business will need for equipment, vehicles or build-out in the first few years.

anchors.1: Major equipment, vehicles or build-out due soon, at a cost that eats a year of earnings or more.
anchors.3: Normal ongoing replacement; nothing big due.
anchors.5: Little equipment, or recent major upgrades already done.

criteria.brokerQ: Age and condition of major equipment and vehicles? Any big replacements or repairs expected in the next 3 years?

criteria.name: Competitive position
criteria.hint: Could a new competitor or a big chain take the customers? Judge from evidence, not the broker's adjectives.

anchors.1: Crowded market, easy to copy, competing mostly on price.
anchors.3: Some competition, with a reason customers choose this one (location, service, niche).
anchors.5: A defensible niche, contracts or switching costs that keep customers.

criteria.brokerQ: Who are the main competitors, and why do customers choose this business over them?

criteria.name: Staff stability
criteria.hint: Turnover and how hard the key roles would be to replace.

anchors.1: High turnover, or key staff likely to leave with the owner.
anchors.3: Mixed tenure; a couple of long-time staff.
anchors.5: Long-tenured staff in the key roles, with pay at or above market.

criteria.brokerQ: Staff list with roles, tenure and pay? Are any key employees planning to leave, or related to the owner?

excludedOnPurpose.name: Growth potential / expansion path
excludedOnPurpose.why: Buyers with a bigger vision tend to overpay for deal #1 because of what it could become. The first deal has to stand on its own numbers, so growth plans raise Joy (the 'plan' row), never Fit.

excludedOnPurpose.name: Price vs. typical industry multiple
excludedOnPurpose.why: Deal math already depends on the asking price, so scoring it twice double-counts. The Scorecard shows 'priced rich' / 'priced lean' flags instead.
